name: Fresh Start Effect
description: Temporal landmarks like a new week, month, year, birthday, or return after a lapse can make people feel psychologically separated from past failures and more ready to begin again.
design_relevance_note: Useful in re-engagement, streak repair, goal resets, seasonal campaigns, onboarding restarts, and behavior-change products that time prompts to Mondays, month boundaries, anniversaries, or birthdays.
myth_risk_note: The fresh start effect is documented through multiple empirical studies with real-world behavioral data (search patterns, gym visits, exercise follow-through) and now includes a genuinely independent research team's confirmation of the proposed mechanism (Peetz & Wilson 2012) -- the specific independent-replication gap this entry's myth_risk_note previously flagged. Rated low rather than none because find-fresh-start-effect itself (the foundational archival-data finding) still carries replication_status=undetermined per Phase 27's own replication-audit pass, which found no independent replication of that specific archival-measures paradigm -- Peetz & Wilson confirms the underlying mechanism via a different paradigm, not a direct replication of Dai et al.'s exact study design.
prevalence_note: Now common in behavior-change and retention design: NN/g has a dedicated article on it and practitioner pattern libraries explicitly frame it as a reusable digital-product pattern, even if it is newer than the classic UX canon.

findings.description: People are more likely to pursue goal-directed and aspirational behavior immediately following a temporal landmark — the outset of a new week, month, year, or semester, a birthday, or a holiday — than at other times. Demonstrated across three independent archival measures: Google searches for 'diet' spike after temporal landmarks, university gym visits increase after them, and online goal commitments (stickK.com) cluster immediately after them. Proposed mechanism: landmarks create new mental accounting periods that psychologically separate past imperfections from the present, prompting a 'big-picture' self-view that motivates aspirational action.
findings.source_title: The Fresh Start Effect: Temporal Landmarks Motivate Aspirational Behavior

applications.title: Mint.com pairing a tax-refund landmark with an affiliate investment recommendation
applications.description: Mint.com notifies users when a tax refund arrives and, in the same moment, recommends an affiliate company (Wealthfront) as a way to invest the refund -- using a genuine financial landmark as the occasion to route the user toward a paid partner's product.
applications.ethical_note: This carries a real, worth-naming conflict-of-interest shape: Mint is recommending a named affiliate partner, not a neutral or personalized best option, at a moment chosen specifically because the user is primed to act. The recommendation may genuinely suit the user's stated goal (investing a refund), but the source doesn't establish that Wealthfront was chosen for fit rather than the affiliate relationship, so this is graded mixed rather than user_beneficial.

applications.title: Whittl.com framing a New Year email around a fresh-start narrative
applications.description: Whittl.com's New Year marketing email frames the new year explicitly as a chance for personal reinvention ('New Year. New You.') before recommending a specific service (a salon visit), using a genuine temporal landmark to prime the recipient toward an aspirational self-image the recommended purchase then serves.
applications.ethical_note: The temporal landmark (New Year) is real and shared by everyone, not fabricated -- but pairing it with an aspirational 'new you' narrative to sell a specific paid service is a deliberate emotional lever, not neutral information. Low individual stakes (a salon visit) keep this from graded manipulative_risk.
